full_title: SARIPODEN ARIMAN GURO, PETITIONER, VS. COMMISSION ON ELECTIONS AND SOMERADO MALOMALO GURO, RESPONDENTS.
subject: Political and Public International Law
syllabus_topic: XII. Election Law > E. Remedies and Jurisdiction > 1. Petition to Deny Due Course or Cancel Certificate of Candidacy
topics: Nature of a petition is determined by its grounds, not its caption
25-day period to file a Section 78 petition
Strict application of the period for ineligibility grounds (registered voter, age, residence)
When the COMELEC Rules may be relaxed

other_subjects.subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: V. Special Civil Actions > D. Review of Commission on Elections and Commission on Audit Judgments and Final Orders or Resolutions (Rule 64)

doctrine:
A petition that seeks to disqualify a candidate on the ground of **ineligibility** (here, that he is not a registered voter of the municipality) is in the nature of a **petition to deny due course to or cancel a certificate of candidacy under Section 78 of the Omnibus Election Code**, whatever its caption. It must be filed within the period in Rule 23, Section 2 of the COMELEC Rules of Procedure (as amended by COMELEC Resolution No. 9523): within five days from the last day for filing COCs, but **not later than 25 days from the filing of the COC** being challenged.

Where the alleged ineligibility is misrepresentation as to being a registered voter, the period is **applied strictly**, as with age or residence. The Court relaxes it only in exceptional situations, such as the lack of Philippine citizenship (Aznar; Frivaldo), a supervening event that supplies the ground (Hayudini), or peculiar circumstances showing diligence (Caballero; Ocate). Dismissing a late petition on this ground is not grave abuse of discretion.
facts:
Private respondent Somerado Guro filed his certificate of candidacy (COC) for Municipal Mayor of Lumbaca-Unayan, Lanao del Sur on October 16, 2015 for the May 2016 elections. He stated under oath that he was a registered voter of Barangay Poblacion Dilausan and was eligible for the office.

Petitioner Saripoden Guro, the incumbent mayor running for re-election, filed a "Petition for Disqualification" on April 29, 2016. He alleged that, based on the posted certified voters' list, private respondent was not a registered voter of the municipality and was therefore not qualified to run.

Private respondent answered that the petition was moot: the COMELEC had approved the recommendation of its Election and Barangay Affairs Department to include his name in the supplemental list of voters. He also said he voted on election day and had won and been proclaimed mayor.

The COMELEC First Division dismissed the petition for being filed beyond the 25-day period for a petition under Section 78 of the Omnibus Election Code. The COMELEC En Banc denied reconsideration, found the petition filed "way beyond" the period, and did not reach the other issues. Petitioner went to the Supreme Court on certiorari under Rule 64 in relation to Rule 65, claiming the COMELEC should have decided on the merits instead of on "mere technical grounds."
issues: Whether the petition, captioned as a petition for disqualification but grounded on the candidate's ineligibility, is a Section 78 petition to deny due course to or cancel a COC.
Whether the COMELEC gravely abused its discretion in dismissing the petition for having been filed beyond the reglementary period instead of relaxing its rules and ruling on the merits.
ruling:
**1. Yes, it is a Section 78 petition.** Because the petition was anchored on private respondent's alleged ineligibility, the COMELEC correctly treated it as a petition to deny due course to or cancel his COC under Section 78 of the OEC, governed by Rule 23 of the COMELEC Rules of Procedure as amended by Resolution No. 9523. Rule 23, Section 2 requires filing within five days from the last day for filing COCs, but not later than 25 days from the filing of the COC challenged. Private respondent filed his COC on October 16, 2015; the petition came on April 29, 2016, after "a whopping one hundred ninety-six (196) days."

**2. No grave abuse of discretion.** The Court reviewed the cases where it did not insist on the period. In *Aznar* it ruled on the merits despite a late petition because the issue was citizenship. In *Loong* it explained that a misrepresentation as to age is not on the same level as lack of citizenship, and that where disqualification rests on age, residence, or other grounds of ineligibility, "the reglementary period provided by law should be applied strictly." The Court saw no reason to depart from this rule for an alleged misrepresentation as to being a registered voter.

The cases that relaxed the rules were distinguishable: *Hayudini* (a supervening final RTC ruling deleting the candidate from the voters' list armed the petitioner with the ground), *Caballero* (a residency issue imbued with public interest plus peculiar circumstances excusing defective service), and *Ocate* (a one-day delay caused by a typhoon despite due diligence). **No analogous circumstance existed here, so the COMELEC committed no grave abuse of discretion in dismissing the petition on technical grounds.**
disposition: The petition was DISMISSED. The COMELEC En Banc Resolution dated September 25, 2017 in SPA No. 16-086 (DC), affirming the COMELEC First Division's Order dated October 19, 2016, was AFFIRMED.

bar_questions.q: On October 5, 2024, Pedro filed his certificate of candidacy for municipal mayor, stating under oath that he is a registered voter of the municipality. Five months later, rival candidate Juan filed with the COMELEC a pleading captioned "Petition for Disqualification," alleging only that Pedro is not a registered voter of the municipality and is therefore ineligible. The COMELEC dismissed the petition as filed out of time. Juan argues that his petition is a disqualification case, not a petition to cancel a certificate of candidacy, so the 25-day period does not apply. Is Juan correct?

alac.answer: No, Juan is not correct. His petition is a Section 78 petition to deny due course to or cancel a certificate of candidacy, and it was filed out of time.
alac.legal_basis: The nature of a petition is determined by its grounds, not its caption. A petition anchored on a candidate's ineligibility is a petition to deny due course to or cancel a COC under Section 78 of the Omnibus Election Code. Under Rule 23, Section 2 of the COMELEC Rules of Procedure, as amended by COMELEC Resolution No. 9523, it must be filed within five days from the last day for filing COCs, but not later than 25 days from the filing of the COC challenged. Where the ground is misrepresentation as to being a registered voter, the period is applied strictly. (Guro v. COMELEC, G.R. No. 234345, June 22, 2021)
alac.application: Juan's only ground is that Pedro is not a registered voter, which goes into Pedro's eligibility and the truth of a material representation in his COC. The caption "Petition for Disqualification" does not change its nature; it is a Section 78 petition. It was filed about five months after Pedro filed his COC, far beyond the 25-day limit. Nothing shows an exceptional circumstance, such as a supervening event, that would justify relaxing the rule.
alac.conclusion: The COMELEC correctly dismissed Juan's petition for having been filed beyond the reglementary period.

bar_questions.q: Rosa filed her certificate of candidacy for vice mayor on October 3, 2024, declaring that she is a registered voter of the municipality. Teresa filed a timely petition to deny due course to Rosa's COC, but the COMELEC dismissed it because, on that same day, the MTC granted Rosa's petition for inclusion in the list of voters. On appeal, the RTC reversed the MTC, and the order deleting Rosa from the voters' list became final in March 2025. Teresa immediately filed a second petition to deny due course to Rosa's COC, more than 150 days after Rosa filed her COC. Rosa moves to dismiss, citing the 25-day period. May the COMELEC give due course to Teresa's second petition?

alac.answer: Yes. The COMELEC may relax its rules because a supervening event furnished the ground for the second petition.
alac.legal_basis: The 25-day period for a Section 78 petition under Rule 23, Section 2 of the COMELEC Rules of Procedure is generally applied strictly when the ground is ineligibility such as not being a registered voter. However, the Court has allowed liberal construction where a supervening event affects the substance of the case, as in Hayudini v. COMELEC, where a final RTC ruling deleting the candidate from the voters' list armed the petitioner with the ground for a petition filed 172 days after the COC. In Guro v. COMELEC (G.R. No. 234345, June 22, 2021), the Court reaffirmed strict application but recognized Hayudini as a valid exception because of the supervening event.
alac.application: Unlike in Guro, where the petitioner simply filed late with no special circumstance, Teresa was diligent: she filed a timely first petition, which was dismissed only because of the MTC inclusion order. The RTC's later reversal, which became final, is a supervening event. It gave Teresa a ground she did not have before, and enforcing the first dismissal would be inequitable. These facts mirror Hayudini.
alac.conclusion: The COMELEC may give due course to Teresa's second petition despite the lapse of the 25-day period.

bar_questions.q: The COMELEC En Banc affirmed its First Division's dismissal of Andres's petition to deny due course to a mayoral candidate's COC because the petition was filed 200 days after the COC. Andres wants to bring the case to the Supreme Court, arguing that the COMELEC should have decided the case on the merits rather than on a technicality. (a) What remedy should Andres file, and on what ground? (b) Will the remedy prosper?

alac.answer: (a) A petition for certiorari under Rule 64 in relation to Rule 65 of the Rules of Court, on the ground of grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction. (b) No, it will not prosper.
alac.legal_basis: Judgments, final orders, and resolutions of the COMELEC En Banc are reviewable by the Supreme Court only through certiorari under Rule 64 in relation to Rule 65, which requires a showing of grave abuse of discretion. In Guro v. COMELEC (G.R. No. 234345, June 22, 2021), the Court held that the COMELEC did not gravely abuse its discretion in dismissing, on technical grounds, a Section 78 petition filed 196 days after the COC, because the reglementary period is applied strictly for ineligibility grounds and no circumstance justified relaxing it.
alac.application: Andres must file a Rule 64 petition, alleging grave abuse of discretion by the COMELEC En Banc. But applying a clear reglementary period to a petition filed 200 days late is an exercise of the COMELEC's jurisdiction according to its rules, not a capricious or whimsical act. Absent a supervening event, citizenship issue, or other exceptional circumstance, calling the dismissal a "technicality" does not make it grave abuse of discretion.
alac.conclusion: Andres should file a Rule 64 certiorari petition, but it will be dismissed because the COMELEC committed no grave abuse of discretion.
